certainty_reasoning: Wilde records admiration and nothing further: a description ('a little Italian, Pietro, like a young St John') followed by a declaration in the impersonal conditional ('One would have followed him into the desert'). No approach, no second meeting and no outcome are recorded, which is exactly the desire-expressed shape - direction 'wilde', outcome 'unknown'. This clears the README bar more comfortably than the André clause beside it: a reader who does not hold the coding hypothesis still reads a man saying he would have followed a beautiful young man anywhere, which is a statement about wanting to be near him and not merely a note that he was good-looking. The reading is nonetheless this project's; no scholarly source was consulted. Against a stronger class: romantic-nonsexual would assert a mutual connection the letter does not document - the affect on the page is entirely Wilde's, and Pietro is grammatically the object throughout - and there is no first-person statement of sexual relations for documented-sexual. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a friend. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome, and Pietro's own view of the meeting is not recorded anywhere.
date_label: Met on a three-day trip to Nice with Harold Mellor, reported in a letter the editors date Thursday [? 12 January 1899] from Napoule.
summary: On a three-day excursion from Napoule to Nice with Harold Mellor in January 1899, Wilde met a young Italian named Pietro and wrote to Robert Ross that he was 'like a young St John' and that 'One would have followed him into the desert'. It is the stronger of the two Nice notices - a declaration rather than a description - but it is still only a notice: no surname, no age, no second mention anywhere in the correspondence read, and nothing recorded of what followed.

sources.quote: I met one beautiful person, called André, with wonderful eyes, and a little Italian, Pietro, like a young St John. One would have followed him into the desert.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [? 12 January 1899], Napoule - reporting a three-day trip to Nice with Harold Mellor. 'Him' in the final sentence refers to Pietro; St John is John the Baptist, whence the desert.
sources.supports: The whole of the record for Pietro: a named young Italian met at Nice, compared to a young St John, with Wilde's declaration that one would have followed him into the desert; no outcome recorded
